chapter_title: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring
learning_objective: The learner will infer the likeliest next word for each of five sentence starts and explain that a model completes likely text without looking facts up, with at least 4 of 5 predictions correct on the first attempt and the closing question answered correctly.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** next-word-predictor
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** infer
**Learning Objective:** The learner will infer the likeliest next word for each of five sentence starts and explain that a model completes likely text without looking facts up, with at least 4 of 5 predictions correct on the first attempt and the closing question answered correctly. **Prerequisites:** AI Assistant, Large Language Model (both defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each sentence start the learner commits one of four words before the chances are shown. A prediction is correct when it matches the Likeliest word column in Content. After the fifth prediction the learner answers one closing question. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 predictions and the closing question correct on the first attempt. Viewing the chances is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A language model looks facts up in a database. (2) A model that is usually right is never wrong. (3) A model understands a document it has not been shown. **Instructional Rationale:** Predicting before seeing the answer is the pattern that builds the Understand-level idea that a model continues likely text. The closing question connects the idea to practice: put the source in the prompt. **Content:** The five sentence starts, each with four candidate words and the illustrative chance of each (the chances are made up and are labeled "illustrative"): | # | Sentence start shown to the learner | Candidate words and illustrative chances | Likeliest word | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | The water cycle includes evaporation, condensation, and | precipitation 86%, photosynthesis 5%, erosion 4%, election 0% | precipitation | It is the word that most often follows this list. | | 2 | Rain that does not soak into the ground becomes | runoff 78%, vapor 11%, snow 9%, banana 0% | runoff | It is the usual word for this idea. | | 3 | A watershed is an area of land where all the water drains to the same | place 71%, outlet 19%, river 6%, pencil 0% | place | It is the word that most often completes this phrase. | | 4 | Lake Marlow is fed by the Clearwater River and two smaller | streams 62%, rivers 14%, lakes 5%, cats 0% | streams | The model has never seen Lake Marlow, and "streams" fits the pattern of the sentence. | | 5 | Plants make their food using sunlight, water, and | carbon dioxide 83%, sand 3%, noise 0%, plastic 1% | carbon dioxide | It is the usual completion of this phrase. | The closing question: "Why should you paste the source into the prompt when you ask a model about a resource?" The answer choices: (A) Because the model completes likely text and does not look up facts, so it cannot know what your resource says unless you supply it. (B) Because the model is slow without it. (C) Because the model refuses to answer otherwise. (D) Because pasting makes the answer shorter. The correct answer is A. **Provenance:** The sentence starts are written for this chapter, and the chances are made up, and the sim labels them "illustrative chances, not from a real model". Lake Marlow and the Clearwater River are made up. **Rules:** Each sentence start has exactly one likeliest word, the one with the highest chance. The four candidate words are shown in a shuffled order. The closing question has exactly one correct answer. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one sentence start and four candidate words. 2. The learner chooses the word they think is likeliest, and the choice is committed. 3. The sim shows the chances for all four words, whether the choice was correct, and the Why text. 4. After sentence 5 the sim shows the closing question. 5. The learner answers it, and the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 5 sentence starts in a shuffled order, one attempt each, then one closing question with one attempt. Correct: "Correct: [word]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The likeliest word is [word]. [Why]". The closing question's feedback explains why option A is correct. The summary shows "[n] of 5 predictions and the closing question [correct or missed]". At 4 or more and a correct closing question it adds "You can think like a language model." Otherwise it lists the Why text of each miss. **Starting State:** The first sentence start and four candidate words. The question shown is "Which word is the model likeliest to write next?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter says a language model generates text one piece at a time by predicting what is likely next, that it does not look facts up, and that its worked example gives place a 71 percent illustrative chance after "drains to the same".
